DRI leads CP/M command/file services, operating-system memory and cartridge runtime, shared clipboard storage and bounded I/O scheduling. Logix supplies hardware requirements, boot/recovery firmware, initial mapping and low-level drivers. AION Software develops the TUI and the separate C development environment. Logix leads complete-system acceptance with DRI and AION component qualification.

DRI owns the resulting CP/M version, its CP/M enhancements and the accepted CP/M TUI implementation delivered by AION, with source, documentation and tests. DRI may maintain, modify and license these implementations non-exclusively for other hosts. AION retains its compiler/IDE and pre-existing general-purpose components; any such components included in the delivery carry perpetual rights for DRI to maintain, modify and redistribute them with CP/M. Hardware ownership is not transferred.

AION Software designs and implements the shared text-mode TUI API, controls, editing, menus, forms, lists and pseudo-windows, with C bindings and assembly implementations where appropriate. DRI accepts the source and tests and integrates the implementation into the CP/M system cartridge. Mutable state remains in reserved RAM; applications call shared services rather than embedding another full TUI library.
Support smart devices and expansion cards using Plug and Execute and FlexiBUS technologies, with documented CP/M integration so qualified devices and cards can expose their functions to applications.

DRI adapts CP/M and suitable cartridge code for XIP, separating ROM code/constants from RAM state. Logix supplies mapping hardware and safe boot primitives. Define image headers, entry points, relocation assumptions, RAM initialization, nested calls, callbacks and recovery. Arbitrary existing CP/M binaries are not automatically ROM-executable.

DRI implements user-area support and named groups as explicit extensions to the CP/M 1.4-derived release. Names map to CP/M User Numbers; they do not create hierarchical directories. DRI specifies persistent name metadata, valid names, default selection, enumeration, rename behaviour and compatibility with ordinary CP/M tools before interface freeze.

Logix, DRI and AION jointly maintain the published TUI interface specification. AION retains perpetual rights to reuse, modify and port the delivered TUI source and shared technology for other operating systems and processors, including non-CP/M targets. DRI retains independent CP/M licensing; later improvements require documented compatibility and contribution terms rather than an implied transfer of unrelated software.

DRI owns operating-system bank and cartridge dispatch, preserves caller mappings and stacks, and handles nested calls, interrupts and page-crossing buffers. Stable common-memory code and the system stack remain accessible. Logix owns reset mapping, hardware primitives and controller timing/refresh/DMA behaviour. Installed RAM is distinct from the writable application area advertised before launch; no service silently reduces a running application's TPA.

Logix supplies hardware video drivers and monitor capability discovery. DRI integrates mode selection and supported display services into CP/M, rejecting unsupported configurations. AION implements adaptive TUI layout and rendering over those services, without assuming fixed video addresses or universal 80-column support.

DRI provides clipboard storage/lifecycle and a bounded I/O request service. AION and DRI define clipboard formats and copy/cut/paste semantics. Clipboard and I/O buffers have separate lifetimes and ownership. Define bounds, overflow, persistence, per-device ordering, completion, cancellation, timeouts, errors and flushing; slow devices must not block keyboard service. Standard CP/M calls retain synchronous semantics; this does not introduce foreground multitasking.

Logix owns hardware and cartridge electrical design, address decode and ROM capacity/timing requirements. AION Labs implements and manufactures qualified ROM chips to those requirements under Logix supply arrangements. DRI releases the integrated CP/M image after accepting AION TUI source; Logix controls production image revisions, programming/mask handover and verification with AION Labs. Semiconductor manufacture transfers no software rights.

AION Software develops and owns AION C IDE for Aurelia: integrated editor/build workflow, Z80 C compiler and optimizer, assembler/linker, runtime libraries, TUI bindings, diagnostics, debugging and disk/XIP image tools. The IDE is a separately distributed disk-based offering; the reusable TUI runtime is supplied in the CP/M system cartridge. DRI supplies stable OS interfaces and integration assistance.

Agree interface and calling-convention freezes, source/test/documentation handovers, component acceptance and complete-system qualification before the June 1978 release. DRI funds/staffs its OS work, AION its TUI/IDE work and Logix its platform/integration work, subject to separately documented commercial arrangements. Assign defect ownership by component and jointly triage integration faults. Measure ROM images, stacks, buffers and application RAM; publish supported configurations and replacement/patch procedures. No date alone proves acceptance or manufacturing readiness.

chapters.description:
The system adapts {base_version} for banked-ROM execution while preserving standard entry points, loading conventions and available-memory boundaries. A single foreground application can use ordinary CP/M console/file services; richer behaviour uses the separate versioned Logix API.

The CCP interprets commands and loads disk/cartridge programs; BDOS supplies file services through the machine BIOS, which adapts calls to Logix drivers. Motherboard ROM supplies {firmware_contents}. The system cartridge supplies {cartridge_contents}; command buffers and mutable system state remain in RAM. ROM constants/code must be separated from state and self-modifying routines adapted.

In conventional CP/M, 0000H–00FFH holds vectors, default file-control data and the command/disk buffer. Programs load at {program_load_address} in the transient program area and call BDOS through {bdos_entry}; CCP, BDOS and BIOS occupy higher memory. The TPA is application RAM, not an OS module. Transient editor/copy/assembler/debugger/maintenance utilities load when needed.

Compared with 1.3, the 1.4 base supports four logical drives, BIOS sector translation and extra drive state; BDOS begins one 256-byte page lower while CCP/BIOS bases stay fixed. It revises disk errors, returns DE consistently with HL and splits BDOS into PL/M logic plus an assembly interface. Vanilla 1.4 does not contain Logix banked-ROM, cartridge, dynamic-driver, TUI/clipboard/workspace services or the later CP/M 2.0 disk-parameter-block model.

Logix boot firmware discovers cartridges and provides diagnostics/recovery. The common-memory runtime preserves accessible entry code, stack and interrupt state across nested bank switches, following {memory_model_id}. Drivers in motherboard/device ROM or extensions register video, keyboard, floppy and FlexiBUS services. BIOS and relevant BDOS assumptions must match Aurelia disk formats. DMA uses physical-bank descriptors, bounded transfers and ready handshakes; drain or abort it before warm boot or buffer reuse. Video uploads expose dedicated sprite SRAM and atomic descriptors with backpressure, falling back to programmed I/O where needed.

chapters.chapter_name: Shared TUI ownership and application behaviour
chapters.description:
The system owns {tui_contract_id}, exposed through {portable_api_id} and {display_api_id}. It supplies reusable controls, while {consumer_business_tools_aurelia}, {consumer_abacus_1}, {consumer_abacus_2}, {consumer_bpi_suite} and {consumer_pulse_1} retain their document, calculation, file-management and scheduling logic.

Screen services query usable dimensions, clip/scroll and distinguish document from display coordinates. Compact 40-column and expanded 80-column layouts fit dialogs, names and errors; semantic text/selection/warning roles map to colour or monochrome. Structured character, function/navigation and modifier events support blocking or polled input. Shared fields, lists, menus, forms, popups and focus movement use consistent editing and clipboard commands. Clipboard formats, lengths, capacity, ownership and errors are explicit. Contexts are created/destroyed and activated/deactivated with redraw; one may cover the whole screen. System timing and repeat replace CPU-speed loops.

Sequential applications can use these services without multitasking. Exact widgets, clipboard capacity and workspace reservations remain implementation choices. Preserve legacy console behaviour and stable target ABI, use capability discovery, and avoid hard-coded stride, video addresses, last columns or hardware registers. The same documented API spans Aurelia, Aurelia+ and Artemis; Artemis mediates shared display/clipboard access between processes.

This operating system targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

Adapt both BIOS and relevant BDOS assumptions to Aurelia floppy formats.
Keep bank-switching entry code, stack and critical interrupt handling permanently accessible.
Separate ROM code/constants from RAM state; adapt self-modifying routines.
Discover cartridge/device ROMs through defined, versioned interfaces.
Map Logix peripherals to standard CP/M console, printer and disk services.
Provide a separate versioned Logix service interface and C bindings.
Drivers use bounded DMA transfers with physical-bank descriptors and device-ready handshakes; abort/drain transfers before warm boot or reusing buffers.
Video API exposes dedicated sprite SRAM, atomic descriptor swaps and upload-port backpressure; use programmed I/O fallback where peripherals lack DMA endpoints.
DRI freezes group-name metadata, valid names, default group, enumeration and rename rules while preserving ordinary CP/M tool behaviour.
DRI and AION specify clipboard formats, maximum capacity, overflow, copy ownership and persistence across exit/warm boot. Clipboard storage is separate from in-flight I/O buffers.

DRI specifies request bounds, buffer ownership until completion, cancellation, timeouts, error/flush semantics and recovery. Logix drivers supply completion and device errors; printer traffic cannot block keyboard service.

Measure combined clipboard, I/O, stack and resident-workspace use against the existing 4 KiB lower and 4 KiB common reservations. Revise the advertised TPA before application launch if those allocations are insufficient.
DRI integrates accepted AION TUI code into a versioned ROM image; Logix and AION Labs qualify physical capacity, timing, production image verification and replacement/patch procedures.

chapters.description:
The system adapts {base_version} for banked-ROM execution while preserving standard entry points, loading conventions and available-memory boundaries. A single foreground application can use ordinary CP/M console/file services; richer behaviour uses the separate versioned Logix API.

The CCP interprets commands and loads disk/cartridge programs; BDOS supplies file services through the machine BIOS, which adapts calls to Logix drivers. Motherboard ROM supplies {firmware_contents}. The system cartridge supplies {cartridge_contents}; command buffers and mutable system state remain in RAM. ROM constants/code must be separated from state and self-modifying routines adapted.

In conventional CP/M, 0000H–00FFH holds vectors, default file-control data and the command/disk buffer. Programs load at {program_load_address} in the transient program area and call BDOS through {bdos_entry}; CCP, BDOS and BIOS occupy higher memory. The TPA is application RAM, not an OS module. Transient editor/copy/assembler/debugger/maintenance utilities load when needed.

Compared with 1.3, the 1.4 base supports four logical drives, BIOS sector translation and extra drive state; BDOS begins one 256-byte page lower while CCP/BIOS bases stay fixed. It revises disk errors, returns DE consistently with HL and splits BDOS into PL/M logic plus an assembly interface. Vanilla 1.4 does not contain Logix banked-ROM, cartridge, dynamic-driver, TUI/clipboard/workspace services or the later CP/M 2.0 disk-parameter-block model.

Logix boot firmware discovers cartridges and provides diagnostics/recovery. The common-memory runtime preserves accessible entry code, stack and interrupt state across nested bank switches, following {memory_model_id}. Drivers in motherboard/device ROM or extensions register video, keyboard, floppy and FlexiBUS services. BIOS and relevant BDOS assumptions must match Aurelia disk formats. DMA uses physical-bank descriptors, bounded transfers and ready handshakes; drain or abort it before warm boot or buffer reuse. Video uploads expose dedicated sprite SRAM and atomic descriptors with backpressure, falling back to programmed I/O where needed.

chapters.chapter_name: Shared TUI ownership and application behaviour
chapters.description:
The system owns {tui_contract_id}, exposed through {portable_api_id} and {display_api_id}. It supplies reusable controls, while {consumer_business_tools_aurelia}, {consumer_abacus_1}, {consumer_abacus_2}, {consumer_bpi_suite} and {consumer_pulse_1} retain their document, calculation, file-management and scheduling logic.

Screen services query usable dimensions, clip/scroll and distinguish document from display coordinates. Compact 40-column and expanded 80-column layouts fit dialogs, names and errors; semantic text/selection/warning roles map to colour or monochrome. Structured character, function/navigation and modifier events support blocking or polled input. Shared fields, lists, menus, forms, popups and focus movement use consistent editing and clipboard commands. Clipboard formats, lengths, capacity, ownership and errors are explicit. Contexts are created/destroyed and activated/deactivated with redraw; one may cover the whole screen. System timing and repeat replace CPU-speed loops.

Sequential applications can use these services without multitasking. Exact widgets, clipboard capacity and workspace reservations remain implementation choices. Preserve legacy console behaviour and stable target ABI, use capability discovery, and avoid hard-coded stride, video addresses, last columns or hardware registers. The same documented API spans Aurelia, Aurelia+ and Artemis; Artemis mediates shared display/clipboard access between processes.

This operating system targets Z80/CP/M on {host_base_computer_aurelia} and {host_base_computer_aurelia_plus}. The recorded installed-RAM requirement is {minimum_ram_kib} KiB. The software image is supplied in its matching physical ROM cartridge; hardware construction belongs to that cartridge. Application workspace and ROM footprint remain unspecified.

Split for separate review and authorization at the user's request; before/after contents are preserved from the original proposal. Approve the prerequisite groups first or together.
